sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that the discriminant of the factor [MATH: x^2+x+2] is [MATH: \mathcal D = 1^2-4(1)(2) = -7 < 0] so our cubic cannot be factored any further over the real numbers.

Now, we sketch the graph of the cubic. From the equation, we conclude the following:

  • The graph has an [MATH: x]-intercept at [MATH: x=3.]

  • [MATH: y \to \infty] as [MATH: x \to \infty] and [MATH: y \to -\infty] as [MATH: x \to -\infty.]

  • The [MATH: y]-intercept is [MATH: y|= (0 − 3)(0^{2} + 0 + 2); = (− 3) ⋅ (2); = − 6.]

The corresponding partial graph is shown below.

We are interested in the points [MATH: (a,b)] whose [MATH: x]-coordinate [MATH: a] satisfies [MATH: 1 \leq a \leq 3.] The corresponding interval on the [MATH: x]-axis is highlighted on the graph. Notice that in this interval, the graph of the cubic lies below the [MATH: x]-axis. So, we must have [MATH: b \leq 0.]

Among the given options, only option III does NOT satisfy this condition.

Write the equation that could represent the graph shown in the [MATH: xy]-plane?

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)

sections.normalized_html:
First, we notice that the function has three distinct roots, [MATH: x = -4,] [MATH: x = 0,] and [MATH: x = 3.]

Based on the graph, we can make the following conclusions about the multiplicities of the roots:

  • The graph is not tangent to the [MATH: x]-axis at [MATH: x = -4.] Therefore, this root is simple (the multiplicity equals [MATH: 1]).

  • The graph touches the [MATH: x]-axis and reverses direction at [MATH: x = 0.] Therefore, this root has even multiplicity.

  • The graph is not tangent to the [MATH: x]-axis at [MATH: x = 3.] Therefore, this root is simple (the multiplicity equals [MATH: 1]).

Therefore, the equation we need to find has the form [MATH: f(x) = a(x + 4)x^n(x - 3),] where [MATH: n] is an even natural number.

Of the given options, the following are similar to the form described above: [MATH: f(x)|= (1)/(3)(x + 4)x^{2}(x − 3),; f(x)|= − (1)/(3)(x + 4)x^{2}(x − 3)]

From the diagram, we can notice that the value of the function at [MATH: x=1] is negative, that is, [MATH: f(1) \lt 0.]

  • For [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3),] we have [MATH: f(1)|= (1)/(3)(1 + 4)(1)^{2}(1 − 3); = − (10)/(3); < 0.]

  • For [MATH: f(x) = -\dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3),] we have [MATH: f(1)|= − (1)/(3)(1 + 4)(1)^{2}(1 − 3); = (10)/(3); ≮0.]

Therefore, we discard [MATH: f(x) = -\dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3).]

Consequently, the equation that could represent the graph shown is [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3).]

Explanation:
First, we notice that the function has three distinct roots, [MATH: x = -4,] [MATH: x = 0,] and [MATH: x = 3.]

Based on the graph, we can make the following conclusions about the multiplicities of the roots:

- The graph is not tangent to the [MATH: x]-axis at [MATH: x = -4.] Therefore, this root is simple (the multiplicity equals [MATH: 1]).
- The graph touches the [MATH: x]-axis and reverses direction at [MATH: x = 0.] Therefore, this root has even multiplicity.
- The graph is not tangent to the [MATH: x]-axis at [MATH: x = 3.] Therefore, this root is simple (the multiplicity equals [MATH: 1]).

Therefore, the equation we need to find has the form
[MATH: f(x) = a(x + 4)x^n(x - 3),]
where [MATH: n] is an even natural number.

Of the given options, the following are similar to the form described above:
[MATH: f(x)|= (1)/(3)(x + 4)x^{2}(x − 3),; f(x)|= − (1)/(3)(x + 4)x^{2}(x − 3)]

From the diagram, we can notice that the value of the function at [MATH: x=1] is negative, that is, [MATH: f(1) \lt 0.]

- For [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3),] we have
[MATH: f(1)|= (1)/(3)(1 + 4)(1)^{2}(1 − 3); = − (10)/(3); < 0.]
- For [MATH: f(x) = -\dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3),] we have
[MATH: f(1)|= − (1)/(3)(1 + 4)(1)^{2}(1 − 3); = (10)/(3); ≮0.]

Therefore, we discard [MATH: f(x) = -\dfrac{1}{3}(x + 4)x^2(x - 3).]
